title: SC junks contempt petition vs Tito Sotto over Sara Duterte impeach ruling

blocks.text: MANILA, Philippines — The Supreme Court has dismissed an indirect contempt petition filed against Sen. Tito Sotto over his criticisms of a high court ruling on the impeachment proceedings of Vice President Sara Duterte.

In a statement on Tuesday, October 13, the Supreme Court en banc ruled that Sotto’s public criticisms of the court’s decision in Duterte v. House of Representatives et al. (G.R. Nos. 278353 and 278359) fall within the bounds of protected free speech and expression.

The case stemmed from media interviews and social media posts in which Sotto questioned the ruling, claiming that the ponente was unfamiliar with congressional rules and arguing that the decision effectively amended the Constitution.

Petitioner Manuelito Delos Reyes Luna and several others asked the high court to cite the lawmaker for indirect contempt under Rule 71, Section 3(d) of the Rules of Court, alleging that his remarks were highly disrespectful and threatened to erode public trust in the Judiciary.

The Supreme Court, however, stressed that the Judiciary remains subject to public scrutiny and that statements concerning public officials in the discharge of their duties are protected under the doctrine of fair comment.
“The guarantee of free speech was enacted to protect not only polite speech, but even in its most unsophisticated form,” the court’s ruling read.
The court added that “political speech is accorded the greatest degree of protection” as a direct exercise of popular sovereignty.

To determine whether the speech surpassed constitutional boundaries, the high court evaluated the totality of the circumstances, including the nature of the message, the speaker’s identity, the medium, and its actual impact.

Addressing the modern digital landscape, the court observed that social media algorithms can amplify content, take statements out of context, and spread falsehoods. In light of these realities, the Court noted that it was adopting a "more egalitarian approach" to evaluating speech restrictions, acknowledging unequal access to public platforms.

Because Sotto’s statements involved political discourse, the Supreme Court said it applied the incitement test, which it described as the strictest standard in contempt cases involving speech, to examine whether the remarks intentionally incited the public to lose faith in judicial independence or obstruct justice.
The tribunal held that Sotto’s comments presented no such danger and did not meet the threshold under the clear and present danger test.

“In contempt cases involving speech, the SC explained that the key question is whether the statements intentionally incite the public to lose trust in the independence of the Judiciary or to obstruct the administration of justice, and whether, considering the totality of circumstances, there is a likelihood and imminence that the statements will produce these effects,” the Supreme Court’s statement read.
The high court held that Sotto’s public disagreement with the impeachment decision and its ponente formed part of a legitimate public debate on an issue of national importance.
While acknowledging Sotto’s significant reach and influence as a public figure, the court pointed out that his remarks were made primarily in response to reporters’ questions.
“There is no showing he intended to incite or rally the public to lose trust in the independence of the Judiciary,” the decision said, according to the high court’s statement.
“There is no sign of bad faith or malice,” it added.

The high court cautioned that penalizing public figures for expressing disagreement with judicial rulings would unduly stifle free expression, emphasizing that discussions on impeachment proceedings must remain unrestricted by fear of subsequent punishment.

“As a matter of paramount public interest, discussions on impeachment proceedings, including opinions critical of the court’s decisions, should be free and unrestricted by fears of subsequent punishment,” the high court said.
